#9443. Are You Making This Common Mistake With Grief?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In recent years, the language of therapy has moved beyond the clinic and into everyday conversation, giving us new ways to name our inner lives and, at times, new ways to misread them. Nowhere is this more evident than in how we respond to grief.

In grief, we learn quickly which words help and which ones wound. “At least they lived a long life.” “They wouldn’t want you to be sad.” Most of us recognize these as unhelpful sentiments.

Not all harmful responses to grief sound like clichés, though. Sometimes they arrive dressed in compassion, wrapped in the language of awareness. A friend might say, “This seems to be activating your abandonment wound,” “Maybe this pain is really about your father,” or “Maybe this is more about your unhappiness in your marriage.” The words may be well-intentioned, even psychologically accurate, yet the effect can be deeply unsettling. Instead of feeling seen, we feel studied; instead of comforted, diagnosed.

This dynamic can feel like a kind of gaslighting because the tools and language of healing are used to explain away your emotions instead of tending to them. Unlike gaslighting in the usual sense, it isn’t malicious. It’s the experience of being told what your pain really means instead of having that pain simply met. It is a byproduct of a therapy-literate culture that often privileges interpretation over presence.

For the past several years, I’ve taught death and dying at the university level and led grief retreats. Again and again, I’ve watched grief ease, not when someone explained it, but when someone stayed with it. In what follows, I’ll look at how analysis can crowd out presence, and offer ways to stay with grief, someone else’s or your own, without rushing to interpret it.

When we’re grieving, people want to help, but few things wound more than having sorrow dissected while it’s still unfolding. Well-meaning insight can become a form of distance. A loved one may believe they’re offering understanding when they say, “This loss must be reminding you of when you lost your job,” or “You seem to struggle with change, don’t you?,” yet the grieving heart hears something different: that the pain belongs to something older and is therefore less legitimate.

Both can be true. A new loss often awakens older ones, but truth without warmth is just analysis. The body doesn’t sort its ache into past and present; it simply calls for accompaniment. In one well-known study, holding the hand of a trusted person calmed the brain’s response to threat, no words required. Seeing where a present loss touches earlier wounds can be deeply healing, eventually. But categorizing pain does not lessen the need to feel it.

We can also engage in this kind of gaslighting internally. Once we have absorbed enough psychological language, we can turn the same clinical lens on ourselves. We catch the echo of a past wound and then scold our grief for being disproportionate. “I’m overreacting,” we tell ourselves. “This is just my old stuff.” “Why can’t I just be happy?” Yet grief does not care how insightfully we label it. It still needs space to breathe. Awareness can be a form of care, but only when it does not rush ahead of the feeling itself. If it becomes a strategy to bypass feeling, our own or another’s, it defeats itself.

Many guests arrive at our retreats saying some version of “I should be over this by now.” Over the days that follow, that urgency to be finished often quiets, not through argument, but because the grief is finally given room. On the last day, they complete a ritual deep in the forest, at a fountain carved with the outline of a family. Around it, they leave rocks painted with the names of the people they’ve lost. The oldest rocks have since faded almost past recognition, the paint softening into a weathered imprint.

I’ve come to see this not as loss, but as integration: the sharp color of a fresh wound, still seeking an explanation, settling into something that no longer needs to announce itself. No one stood over the rocks interpreting them. They simply bore witness. Grief often becomes more endurable in exactly this way: when it is allowed to change shape in the space of time, care, and presence.

These suggestions come from years of sitting with grieving people, and from my own experience of loss. They are less techniques than reminders of what the moment is asking for.

Resist the urge to explain. The interpretive reflex—reaching for meaning, context, or psychological framing—is often a response to our own helplessness in the face of grief’s rawness. Notice when you’re doing it, pause, and return to the simpler question: Can I be here with this person, without needing it to mean something right now?

Let the silence be full rather than empty. Many people fill silence because it feels like abandonment. A silence in which you remain present, your body in the room, your attention undivided, can be the most companioning thing you offer. “I’m here,” said once and then honored, is worth more than 10 minutes of careful insight.

Follow their lead on meaning. If the grieving person begins to find meaning themselves, to name connections, to speak about what this loss is touching in their past, that is theirs to do. Your role is to witness it, not to initiate it. There is a world of difference between meaning that emerges from the griever and meaning that is handed to them. When you catch yourself doing it, try asking a different question: What does this need? Usually the answer is simpler than any interpretation: company, time, permission to be exactly this intense.

If you feel the pull to theorize about someone else’s grief, a few questions can help you track it in time: Am I trying to ease their pain, or my own discomfort with it? Did they ask for insight, or am I offering it uninvited? Have I acknowledged the loss itself, fully, before reaching for what it might mean?

When you’re unsure what to say, three phrases rarely go wrong: “Tell me about them.” “What do you miss most today?” “I’m here.” Each one keeps the person grieving at the center.

Grief has a way of making us distrust our own experience. We begin measuring whether we’re grieving correctly, whether we’ve stayed sad too long or not long enough, or whether the intensity means something beyond the loss itself.

Catch the self-diagnosis. This one is not easy, because the narrating voice sounds so reasonable: “This is really about my mother,” “I’m being too sensitive,” “I’m being disproportionate.” It rarely announces itself as unkind.

Notice when you’re applying the same analytical approach to yourself that you’d resist from someone else. Then let the intensity of the feeling stand without demanding it justify itself first.

Ask your grief what it needs, not what it means. Meaning can come later, if it comes at all. In the acute moment, the more honest question is practical: You might need rest, someone to call, permission to cancel a plan. Let the meaning-making wait.

Choose your witnesses. Some people simply cannot stay in the uncertainty that grief creates. Their discomfort shows up as advice, reassurance, or psychological evaluation. It doesn’t make them uncaring. It simply means they may not be the people to rely on in the rawest moments of loss. Notice who can sit in the room without needing to fix or explain, and lean on them more.

Insight has a place in grief. In time, many people do come to see how one loss is woven through the others, and that understanding can bring relief. But it tends to arrive on its own schedule, after the pain has been felt and met. Until then, what we can offer, to someone else or to ourselves, is company. The rocks at the fountain didn’t fade because anyone explained them. They faded because they were left where they were, held by time and by the people who stood beside them. Even when a wound is old, the tenderness it requires is always immediate.

Naomi Sanderovsky, Ph.D., is the founder of Luma Via retreats and trainings, and the creator of Living Grief Theory and Felt Sense Dynamics. She has taught world religions, global philosophy, and more recently death and dying at the university level for more than 20 years.

Children know the deepest truths about life, the elemental knowledge we unlearn in the act of living, those inarticulable truths music alone helps us remember. To hear children sing the secret wisdom of the heart is to be in the presence of something truer and more transcendent than any of our poems and postulates can touch — the ultimate affirmation of our aliveness, emanating Richard Powers’s beautiful and bittersweet assertion that “the use of music is to remind us how short a time we have a body.”

To celebrate twenty years of The Marginalian, composer extraordinaire Paola Prestini set six of her favorite bird divinations to music, which the Young People’s Chorus of New York City brought to life with their commanding innocence and their tender power. Paola’s perfect title for the piece, drawn from one of the cards, captures what every child is when this world is worth of its children: “Meteor of Joy.”

Couple with another choir of young people accompanying David Byrne’s anthem of faith in life, “One Fine Day,” then revisit the story and process behind these bird divinations.

#9441. Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

For people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain. Now, scientists have discovered that these painful episodes activate a surprising part of the brain, one closely connected to our sense of identity and how we think about ourselves.

Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain. The discovery suggests that persistent back pain may become deeply intertwined with a person's sense of self, potentially helping explain why conventional pain treatments often provide limited relief.

According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. When pain persists for more than 12 weeks, it is considered chronic. For many patients, everyday movements can provoke sudden flare-ups that make an already difficult condition even harder to manage.

Although the brain plays a central role in how pain is experienced, researchers have struggled to identify the precise brain circuits responsible for pain triggered by movement.

Chronic Back Pain Activates the Brain's Sense of Self

The new study, published on October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, identified an unexpected response involving the brain's Default Mode Network (DMN).

Sometimes called the "self network," the DMN consists of interconnected regions in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These areas are especially active when our attention turns inward, such as when we reflect on personal experiences, think about our identity, or consider our thoughts and emotions. In contrast, the network generally becomes less active when we direct our attention toward something happening around us.

The researchers discovered that sudden back pain caused by movement switched this network on rather than off. This unusual response suggests that chronic pain involves more than the processing of physical sensations. It may also engage the brain systems that shape how people experience themselves.

The findings could help researchers understand why treatments that focus primarily on suppressing pain symptoms do not always work well for chronic low back pain. They also raise the possibility that targeting the DMN could offer a different approach to treatment.

Brain Scans Reveal a Surprising Difference Between Chronic and Acute Pain

To investigate what happens in the brain during a pain flare, the researchers recruited 114 patients with chronic low back pain.

Each participant completed a "leg raise test," a standard clinical procedure used to provoke back pain. During the test, researchers monitored changes in brain blood flow using a specialized functional MRI method called arterial spin labeling. This technique allows scientists to track patterns of brain activity by measuring blood flow without relying on an injected contrast agent.

The team also examined how participants responded to a separate painful stimulus. They applied a harmless but uncomfortable heat sensation to the calf, similar to the brief pain someone might experience when accidentally touching a hot stove.

Comparing these two situations revealed a striking difference.

When movement triggered a flare of chronic back pain, the DMN became more active. However, when participants experienced the painful heat stimulus, the same network became less active, following the brain's typical response to acute pain.

The researchers also identified several other important patterns:

Together, these findings provide new evidence that chronic pain flares involve brain processes associated with personal identity, not just the physical experience of pain.

Why the Brain Reacts Differently to Chronic Pain

During ordinary acute pain, the brain generally reduces activity in the DMN so it can concentrate on the immediate source of danger. This response helps shift attention away from internal thoughts and toward an external threat.

But the UC San Diego researchers found that movement triggered chronic back pain produced the opposite effect.

"In every pain study, when you're experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates," said corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, PhD, professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, endowed professor at the Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and director of the Pain Health and Mindfulness Laboratory at UC San Diego School of Medicine. "What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are."

The findings suggest that chronic back pain can become closely connected with the brain's internal representation of the self. Rather than processing pain solely as a physical warning signal, the brain may also link it to personal memories, expectations, and emotional experiences.

For someone living with chronic pain, this means the experience can extend far beyond the moments when the pain is physically present. Worry about the next flare, memories of previous episodes, and fear of movements that might trigger pain can all become part of everyday life.

"The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It's contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain."

This connection between pain and personal identity may help explain why chronic back pain can be especially difficult to treat.

A New Direction for Chronic Back Pain Treatment

Because movement-triggered chronic back pain engages different brain networks from ordinary acute pain, researchers believe traditional treatments may fail to address some of the processes that sustain the experience of chronic pain.

Medications such as opiates primarily target pain signaling, but they may not adequately address the brain networks involved in the emotional and personal dimensions of persistent pain.

"Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that's not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one's identity."

The discovery points toward treatments that address not only the sensation of pain but also the brain's relationship with that sensation.

Recent work by Zeidan and his colleagues has explored two potential approaches: mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin.

Both approaches are being investigated for their ability to help people experience physical pain without allowing it to become as closely tied to their identity. Early findings suggest that changing this relationship may reduce pain intensity, although additional research is needed to confirm the results and determine how effective these treatments may be.

"These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person," Zeidan said. "Mindfulness is a meditation technique that's about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They're not a silver bullet -- you're not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you're changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn't contaminate your everyday life."

Can Mindfulness and Psychedelics Change How the Brain Experiences Pain?

Rather than attempting to eliminate every pain signal, these approaches aim to change how the brain interprets and responds to the experience.

Mindfulness meditation encourages people to observe their thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations without immediately judging or reacting to them. Psilocybin, meanwhile, is being studied for its potential to alter brain processes that connect pain with earlier experiences, emotional distress, and expectations about the future.

The goal is not necessarily to remove pain altogether, but to reduce how much it influences a person's thoughts, emotions, and daily functioning.

Zeidan's laboratory is currently conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to investigate whether mindfulness meditation and psychedelic treatments can change the neural processes involved in self-reflection. Researchers hope to determine whether these approaches can reshape brain activity and improve how people subjectively experience chronic pain.

Although the research remains at an early stage, the findings offer a different way to think about persistent back pain. Understanding why the brain connects chronic pain with a person's sense of self could eventually help scientists develop treatments that address aspects of pain that conventional therapies often miss.

Additional study authors from UC San Diego School of Medicine include Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Reigner, and Thomas Liu.

Funding was provided in part by the National Institutes of Health's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (Grant #R01AT009693) and the UC San Diego Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion. The researchers reported no conflicts of interest.

Compound interest is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and for good reason. It is the mathematical force that turns consistent, modest investing into life-changing wealth — and it is the foundation of every financial independence plan.

Here is the core concept. Simple interest earns a return only on your original deposit. If you invest $10,000 at 7% simple interest, you earn $700 per year — every year, forever, on the same $10,000 base. After 30 years, you would have $31,000.

Compound interest earns a return on your original deposit plus all the interest previously earned. In Year 1, you earn $700 on your $10,000. In Year 2, you earn 7% on $10,700 — that is $749. In Year 3, you earn 7% on $11,449 — that is $801. Each year, your interest earns its own interest, and the growth accelerates.

After 30 years of compound interest at 7%, your $10,000 grows to approximately $76,123 — more than double the $31,000 from simple interest. And that is with a single $10,000 deposit and no additional contributions.

The difference starts small and then explodes. In the first 10 years, compound interest adds only $2,672 more than simple interest. In the last 10 years (year 20 to 30), it adds over $30,000 more. This accelerating curve is why time in the market matters more than almost any other factor in building wealth.

Investing $500 per month at a 7% average annual return — roughly the inflation-adjusted historical return of the S&P 500 — produces dramatically different results depending on how long you invest. After 10 years: $86,500. After 20 years: $260,500. After 30 years: $567,000. You contribute $180,000 of your own money over 30 years. Compound interest adds $387,000 — more than double your contributions. Time is the multiplier that no amount of additional savings can replace.

The compound interest formula is straightforward once you understand the components:

For a $10,000 investment at 7% compounded monthly for 30 years:

A = 10,000 x (1 + 0.07/12)^(12 x 30) = 10,000 x (1.00583)^360 = $81,165

Notice this is higher than the $76,123 from annual compounding — more frequent compounding produces slightly more growth, though the difference is modest.

The jump from annual to monthly compounding is meaningful. The jump from monthly to daily is negligible. Most bank accounts and investment returns compound daily or monthly, so you are already getting nearly the maximum benefit.

The Rule of 72 is the single most useful mental math shortcut in personal finance. Divide 72 by your expected annual return to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.

At a 7% real return, your money doubles every 10 years. A $100,000 portfolio at age 25 becomes $200,000 at 35, $400,000 at 45, and $800,000 at 55 — even with zero additional contributions. This is why starting early is the single most powerful financial decision you can make.

The following table shows how different monthly contribution amounts grow over time at a 7% average annual return (roughly the inflation-adjusted long-term return of the US stock market). These numbers assume you start with $0 and contribute consistently every month.

Notice the pattern: the growth in the third decade dwarfs the first two decades combined. At $1,000 per month, you accumulate $173,000 in the first 10 years but $613,000 in the last 10 years — with the same monthly contribution. This is compound interest in its most powerful phase.

The 7% figure used above is already adjusted for historical inflation (the nominal S&P 500 return has averaged roughly 10%, minus approximately 3% average inflation). This means the projections above represent real purchasing power — $567,000 in 30 years would buy roughly what $567,000 buys today.

If you use a nominal return of 10% instead, the numbers look even more dramatic, but they overstate your future purchasing power. Always use inflation-adjusted returns (6-7%) for retirement planning and real purchasing power comparisons.

Consider two investors. Investor A starts investing $500 per month at age 25 and stops at age 35 — investing for only 10 years, then letting it grow untouched until age 65. Investor B waits until age 35 and invests $500 per month every month from 35 to 65 — investing for 30 years.

Investor A contributes one-third the money and ends up with more at 65. The 10-year head start gave compound interest enough time to overcome the difference. This is not a trick — it is the fundamental math of compounding. Every year you delay costs you more than the money you eventually invest.

The single most important factor in compound interest is time, not amount. Even $100 per month started today beats $500 per month started five years from now over a long enough timeline. Open a brokerage account or increase your 401(k) contribution today.

Pro tip: Automate your contributions so they happen before you see the money in your checking account.

The historical 7-10% average return comes from broad stock market index funds. A total US stock market fund or S&P 500 fund with an expense ratio below 0.10% gives you the full benefit of compound growth without high fees eroding your returns.

When you get a raise, increase your monthly investment by at least half the raise amount. This prevents lifestyle inflation from consuming your additional income and accelerates compound growth.

Pro tip: A 3% annual raise invested means your contributions grow exponentially alongside your investment returns.

Set all your accounts to automatically reinvest dividends. Dividend reinvestment is compound interest within compound interest — your dividends buy more shares, which generate more dividends, which buy more shares.

Market downturns are not a reason to sell — they are the cost of admission for long-term compound growth. Every major market crash in history has been followed by recovery and new highs. Pulling money out during a downturn and reinvesting later is the most reliable way to destroy compound interest.

Pro tip: If seeing your balance drop causes panic, check your portfolio less frequently. Quarterly or annually is enough.

Simple interest is calculated only on your original principal. Compound interest is calculated on your principal plus all previously earned interest. Over long periods, the difference is enormous — $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to $31,000 with simple interest but $76,123 with compound interest.

More frequent compounding produces slightly higher returns, but the difference is small. Monthly compounding at 7% on $10,000 for 30 years yields $81,165 versus $76,123 for annual compounding — a difference of about 6.6%. Most investment accounts compound daily or when dividends are reinvested, so you are already receiving near-optimal compounding.

Yes. Compound interest (more accurately, compound growth) applies to any investment account where your returns are reinvested. In a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account invested in index funds, your gains generate additional gains. Tax-advantaged accounts like Roth IRAs are especially powerful because the compounding occurs entirely tax-free.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10% annually in nominal terms over the past century. Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7%. For conservative planning, use 6-7% to account for inflation. For nominal calculations (not inflation-adjusted), use 9-10%. Using rates above 10% for long-term projections is overly optimistic for a diversified portfolio.

Yes — and the math is surprisingly accessible. Investing $1,000 per month at a 7% real return reaches $1,134,000 in 30 years (you contribute $360,000, compound interest adds $774,000). At $500 per month, you reach $567,000 in 30 years. The key variables are consistent contribution, a reasonable return, and patience.

Compound interest is the mathematical engine behind financial independence. The FI community uses compound growth to accumulate 25x their annual expenses in invested assets (the 4% rule). By saving 50%+ of income and investing in index funds that compound at 7-10% annually, FIRE practitioners can reach financial independence in 10-17 years rather than the traditional 40-year career.

Compound interest is the most powerful wealth-building force available to ordinary investors. The math is unambiguous: $500 per month at 7% becomes $567,000 in 30 years, with compound interest contributing more than twice what you personally invest. The two factors you control — how much you invest and how long you stay invested — matter far more than picking the "right" stocks or timing the market. Start today, invest in low-cost index funds, reinvest all dividends, and do not interrupt the compounding. Time is your greatest asset, and every year you wait costs more than you think.

#9439. The Big Review: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous ★★★★½

“The Met’s prize Jackon Pollock”, Autumn Rhythm: Number 30 (1950), flanked by a pair of Lee Krasner’s collage paintings, Blue Level (1955, left) and Stretched Yellow (1955) Photo: Anna-Marie Kellen; courtesy Metropolitan Museum of Art

He was Jack the Dripper. She was The Wife. That is how it went for artist couples in gender-coded mid-century America (and elsewhere). Yet, Lee Krasner (1908-84) played more than a supporting role in her decade-long marriage to Jackson Pollock (1912-56). When his work eclipsed hers, she remained as committed to her own painting as she was to every aspect of his life—except his infidelity and the alcoholism that in 1956 drove him to his death. Even then, she put her devotion to consequential use in securing his legacy. Now the time has come to fully appreciate hers.

That is the organising principle behind Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, the gorgeous and largely convincing blockbuster at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. While other US museums have previously surveyed the artists separately and in tandem, for the Met curators David Breslin and Brinda Kumar, none gave Krasner, a first-generation Abstract Expressionist, a fair shake.

Their exhibition strives to give a primacy to Krasner’s work that parallels Pollock’s. Note whose name comes first in the show’s title. Its subtitle likewise derives from a Krasner at the she-who-laughs-last finale. What’s more, a dramatically lit, black box of a gallery starts it off with a bracing presentation of six vertical abstractions that Krasner made in the 1950s by collaging cuttings from her unsold paintings with pieces of canvas and bits of Pollock’s drawings punctuated by slashes of pink and orange.

Nonetheless, the eye keeps moving to a window-like opening that functions as a proscenium for the theatre of Pollock’s Convergence: No. 10 (1952), an immense and riveting painting of black paint skeins shot with explosions of colour. Mounted on an angled, freestanding wall in another room, the sight offers viewers a taste of what is in store: signature Pollocks ricocheting off shape-shifting Krasners, and vice-versa.

If only the curators did not show Krasner still riding his coattails. Pollock’s name remains the bigger draw. Ultimately, he still comes off as the bigger trailblazer, and she, his foremost champion, more willing to risk failure to experiment and invent. As Breslin speculated during the press preview: “I don’t think we would have a Jackson Pollock if it weren’t for what Krasner did to support his work.”

There is no way to test that theory, but if Krasner and Pollock proves anything, it is that the artists’ relationship was so codependent that the reverse may be just as true. Yet, today her influence and market value pale before his. Krasner’s auction record, set at Sotheby’s in 2019, is $11.7m for The Eye is the First Circle (1960), one of her larger canvases in the show. That is not chump change, but this year Christie’s sold Pollock’s Number 7A (1948) for $181.2m, an eye-watering price but still short of the reported $200m that financier Ken Griffin paid David Geffen, in 2016, for Number 17A (also 1948).

Photo by Anna-Marie Kellen; courtesy of The Met

Krasner and Pollock met in 1942, when she was better-known to the Abstract Expressionist crowd in New York and Pollock the only unfamiliar name in a show of American and European Modernists (partially recreated at the Met) that the painter John Graham organised and included works by both. By linking their small, vibrant abstractions with works by Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Henri Matisse, Amadeo Modigliani, Giorgio de Chirico and Willem de Kooning, the show virtually jumpstarted their careers. It also made them a couple.

Krasner introduced herself in a spontaneous visit to Pollock’s studio and was so dazzled that she hit a creative block. That did not stop them from dating. He was a Midwestern former student of Thomas Hart Benton in thrall to Picasso and Mexican muralists. She was inspired by Arshile Gorky’s abstractions and Matisse’s cut-outs. Soon he was importing a Matissean palette to his painting and showing at Peggy Guggenheim’s Art of this Century gallery. Sales were not brisk. Pollock’s drinking was more prodigious. Krasner insisted they marry and move to Springs, in East Hampton—to protect him from himself—and persuaded Guggenheim to cover the downpayment.

Relocating did the trick for three unusually sober years—long enough for Pollock to produce his breakthrough drip paintings and achieve lasting fame, before settling, intermittently, into new bouts of alcoholism and depression; a creative paralysis set in. Krasner’s career took off, with a confident 1955 solo show at New York’s Stable Gallery.

Breslin and Kumar take care not to place the artists’ works close together, so Krasner’s modestly-scaled paintings can hook the eye without being overwhelmed by Pollock’s volatile monumentalism. Until she was widowed and took over Pollock’s now-famous barn, Krasner worked in their kitchen and he in an upstairs bedroom. Two contiguous galleries, both painted black, approximate the size of the artists’ studios and distill the show’s thesis with luminous economy, leading viewers from the lyrical, early choreography of his pours, drips and stains to her smaller but exquisite Little Images—mosaic-like geometries painted with a palette knife.

From these sepulchral chambers the show opens to a large, high-ceilinged gallery flooded with daylight from newly revealed windows on Central Park. Here, Convergence hangs, backed with the Met’s prize Pollock, Autumn Rhythm: Number 30 (1950). The operatic shift in tone and scale drives home the outsize renown Pollock achieved after a 1949 feature in Life magazine posed the question, “Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?”

In the same gallery, tellingly, the eight collage paintings Krasner showed at Stable Gallery turn from the Pollocks to face each other like the stones of Stonehenge and look just as ritualistic, if more elated. After that, it’s back to black for a segment titled Re:Echo (after a Krasner), where Pollock’s arabesque, later works hang near her Robert Motherwell-like abstractions of the same period.

The rest of the show is all Krasner, but she outlived Pollock by 28 years. The swirling, abstracted floral landscapes became monumental, but appear in a few too many galleries, homogenizing their visual impact. The point—that no full understanding of one artist can come without the other—has already been made, capped by the one side-by-side juxtaposition: The Deep (1953), a chilling canvas where Pollock nearly obliterated a dark biomorph in clouds of white, and Birth (1956), an image of interlocking pink and black forms that Krasner painted the year he died. That pairing said it all.

Will this show correct a historic imbalance? Probably not market-wise, but a reputational correction seems both necessary and likely.

Installation view including Pollock's The Deep (1953)and Krasner's Birth (1956) in Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous

Photo by Anna-Marie Kellen; courtesy of The Met

The New York Times’s Holland Cotter describes the exhibition as an “exercise of art-historical reset”, and calls its installation of Pollocks “an entrancing sight”, while exulting in the “distinctive impression of personal joy” in Krasner’s post-Pollock work. In The Wall Street Journal, Karen Wilkin applauds the curators for encouraging “concentration on their work, rather than the mythology attached to both painters”, and on her Instagram, Jasper Johns’s biographer Deborah Solomon raves: “It’s like holding two opposed thoughts in your brain at the same time and wondering if your head will explode from the exhilaration of it all.”

In 1824, studying a set of large fossil bones discovered in a quarry near Oxford two centuries earlier, the English theologian, geologist, and paleontologist William Buckland kept looking at the fragment of the lower jaw. Something didn’t add up. As he examined it more closely, he realized these were not the remains of an elephant, as previously thought, but of an enormous carnivorous reptile with no analogue in the fossil record or in the living world.

He christened it Megalosaurus — the first named dinosaur — and set out to compose a complete account of the ancient beast.

Because nobody knew what dinosaurs looked like, he needed an exceptional scientific illustrator whose unbridled imagination and disciplined draughtsmanship could enflesh the bones of the mysterious creature. Taken by a particularly excellent drawing of the jaw of an extinct hyena, he obtained a letter of introduction to the artist, tucked it into his coat pocket, and boarded a coach across Devonshire, hoping to be received.

William took one book to accompany him on the long ride — a weighty new volume by paleontology founding father Georges Couvier, summarizing his pioneering research on the fossil bones of quadrupeds. With gaping disbelief, he watched another passenger take out that same book and begin paging through it. The conversation was inevitable and the realization quick: She was the artist he was traveling to meet. Cuvier himself had sent her the book in gratitude for her contribution.

Perhaps because she had lost her mother while still an infant, Mary Morland had grown up fascinated by deep time, by the slow-burning beauty of minerals, by the way fossils immortalized the ephemerality of the flesh. After devouring Couvier’s books as a teenager, she taught herself draughtsmanship and unlearned what her culture had told her she could be: Determined to become an artist of science, she sent her specimen illustrations to Couvier himself.

The venerable scientist was so taken with the young woman’s work that he published it alongside his studies. Word spread across the scientific community and soon she was illustrating other books and modeling rare specimens in leather.

Unlike most women of her time, whose standard path to subsistence was marriage, Mary could now make a living by her own work. If she married, it would only be for love. Her love was the science of time: She kept drawing paleontological specimens, grew an impressive mineral collection, became a fossil geologist herself.

By the time she met William that day on the coach, she was an old maid in her late twenties and one of the era’s most esteemed scientific illustrators. They started on the dinosaur work immediately.

Within a year, Mary Morland was Mary Buckland. Their home became a miniature Alexandria of science books, light pouring in from candle-holders made of ichthyosaurus vertebrae, fossils lining every sideboard. Their dining room housed a menagerie of frogs and snakes. Guinea pigs ran regularly across the table. A pony occasionally rode past, a laughing child on its back.

One of their surviving children would later recount that Mary not only illustrated William’s studies but, with her “great mental powers, habits of perseverance and order, tempered by excellent judgment,” she “gave to them a polish which added not a little to their merit.”

Despite their fourteen-year age difference, she outlived him by just over a year, channeling her bereavement in studying marine bryozoans — coral-like saltwater creatures — with her daughter. Hours before her death, Mary was still bent over her microscope, entranced by a new specimen.

Mary and William were buried alongside one another, their entwined fossils to be discovered by some paleontologist of the far future: What is love if not the mutual belonging of our passions and our bones.

#9437. Can Well-Being Give You Two More Years of Life?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Decades of scientific inquiry have found that the quality and length of a person’s life goes up when they experience less depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions. More recent studies of psychological well-being—also referred to as happiness, flourishing, thriving, or the good life (among other terms)—have been reporting positive links to health and longevity.

For many, this combination of findings raises a question: “Does human mortality depend on the presence of human happiness and flourishing, or merely on the absence of mental health symptoms or bad feelings?”

That’s what Max Genecov and David S. Yeager explored in a recent meta-analysis, which combined findings from 99 different studies that measured mental health symptoms and conditions, well-being scores, and lifespan. Importantly, all the studies that they drew from used a longitudinal method, which means they took measurements repeatedly over time to explore whether momentary scores or score changes over time (e.g., well-being in early adulthood, or improvement in well-being) correspond with later scores or changes in another factor (such as the age or cause of death).

Well-being is generally understood as a combination of regularly feeling positive emotions, being satisfied with your life, and having a sense of meaning and purpose in life; ill-being reflects frequent and persistent negative emotions, chronic dissatisfaction, and purposelessness.

To get at this question of whether mental ill-being and well-being over time had overlapping, combined, or independent effects on all-cause mortality, Genecov and Yeager used a statistical approach that allowed them to correct for multiple factors under consideration. Their method was able to mathematically enumerate the impact of well-being on mortality while subtracting any coexisting impact of mental health challenges on mortality.

Why? Because if well-being and ill-being exist on a continuum, where reducing mental health conditions is ultimately the same as increasing well-being, then subtracting out the effects of ill-being would erase any concurrent benefit of higher well-being to mortality. But, if improving well-being and reducing ill-being independently affect mortality, where deteriorating mental health conditions and rising well-being contribute separately to how long a person lives, then their model would show distinct advantages of higher well-being to longevity above and beyond reducing symptoms of ill-being.

The result? In this study, people with higher-than-average well-being did live longer—and, indeed, this effect occurs above and beyond the lifespan advantages of lower-than-average ill-being. As the researchers sum up their results:

People one standard deviation above the average on well-being die at a 14% slower rate than those with average well-being. . . . As a practical reference using death probabilities from a 2020 United States Social Security Administration actuarial life table, a standard deviation increase on well-being corresponds to just under two years of more life for both men and women.

They saw older adults and patient populations with greater well-being live longer, and they also found people living longer who rated high in optimism, life satisfaction, positive emotion, a sense of social support, and purpose in life. This result isn’t new in the research, but by looking at the effects of ill-being, they were able to clarify its relationship to well-being and longevity. In fact, Genecov and Yeager found that the lifespan boost documented in their study (which controlled for the possible benefits of alleviating ill-being) was comparable to other studies of well-being and longevity that didn’t control for ill-being. This suggests that prior studies have also been capturing the unique and separate benefit of well-being to health and longevity.

While easy to grasp why, for example, less chronic stress would lead to better cardiovascular health and so a longer life, it’s not as clear from a scientific perspective why or how better overall well-being could help someone live longer. Right now, we know that optimism, positive emotion, social support, and purpose are associated with a longer life—we’re just not sure why, exactly.

That said, there are many ways mental well-being could fuel a longer and better life. More optimistic people, for example, tend to make healthier choices around physical exercise and diet, and to not smoke cigarettes. Positive emotions are linked to investing more effort toward and pursuing goals in life. People who score higher on measures of well-being are more socially appealing, generous, and compassionate toward others, and enjoy higher-quality friendships. One of the most famous studies of longevity attributes survival most strongly to supportive social bonds.

While still an emerging science, those findings suggest that well-being and related factors evoke experiences and motivate behaviors that measurably strengthen physical health in life-lengthening ways. While eliminating ill-being may diminish risks, obstacles, and barriers to physical health, fostering well-being may optimize physical systems to enhance stability, efficiency, and strength—both ultimately contributing to longevity but in different, often intersecting, ways.

Want to do more to enhance your well-being? The Greater Good Science Center has an entire website dedicated to supporting people who’d like to increase well-being called Greater Good in Action. You can explore and tinker with over 150 well-being–promoting activities, exercises, and practices drawn from published research, join a four-week Pathway to Happiness program, or try the seven-day Big JOY project.

Emiliana R. Simon-Thomas, Ph.D., is the science director of the Greater Good Science Center, where she directs the GGSC's research fellowship program and serves as a co-instructor of its Science of Happiness and Science of Happiness at Work online courses.

#9436. Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," says Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake."

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow

The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

The new findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

The team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

"Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," says Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance."

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

The study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

“If you can fall in love again and again,” Henry Miller wrote as he contemplated the measure of a life well lived on the precipice of turning eighty, “if you can forgive as well as forget, if you can keep from growing sour, surly, bitter and cynical… you’ve got it half licked.”

Seven years earlier, the great British philosopher, mathematician, historian, and Nobel laureate Bertrand Russell (May 18, 1872–February 2, 1970) considered the same abiding question at the same life-stage in a wonderful short essay titled “How to Grow Old,” penned in his eighty-first year and later published in Portraits from Memory and Other Essays (public library).

Russell places at the heart of a fulfilling life the dissolution of the personal ego into something larger. Drawing on the longstanding allure of rivers as existential metaphors, he writes:

Make your interests gradually wider and more impersonal, until bit by bit the walls of the ego recede, and your life becomes increasingly merged in the universal life. An individual human existence should be like a river — small at first, narrowly contained within its banks, and rushing passionately past rocks and over waterfalls. Gradually the river grows wider, the banks recede, the waters flow more quietly, and in the end, without any visible break, they become merged in the sea, and painlessly lose their individual being.

In a sentiment which philosopher and comedian Emily Levine would echo in her stirring reflection on facing her own death with equanimity, Russell builds on the legacy of Darwin and Freud, who jointly established death as an organizing principle of modern life, and concludes:

The man who, in old age, can see his life in this way, will not suffer from the fear of death, since the things he cares for will continue. And if, with the decay of vitality, weariness increases, the thought of rest will not be unwelcome. I should wish to die while still at work, knowing that others will carry on what I can no longer do and content in the thought that what was possible has been done.

Portraits from Memory and Other Essays is an uncommonly potent packet of wisdom in its totality. Complement this particular fragment with Nobel laureate André Gide on how happiness increases with age, Ursula K. Le Guin on aging and what beauty really means, and Grace Paley on the art of growing older — the loveliest thing I’ve ever read on the subject — then revisit Russell on critical thinking, power-knowledge vs. love-knowledge, what “the good life” really means, why “fruitful monotony” is essential for happiness, and his remarkable response to a fascist’s provocation.

#9434. Your Prototype Is Not Being Honest With Your Users (And Here’s How To Fix It)

Eric is a Creative Technologist at ProtoPie, where he pushes the boundaries of no-code prototyping. With a background in FinTech UX design, he brings firsthand … More about Eric ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at ProtoPie who help users turn their ideas into highly interactive animations and prototypes for mobile, desktop, web, and IoT. Thank you!

There’s a moment in almost every usability session where a participant pauses at the login screen, types something, and glances up: checking whether they’re “doing it right.” That pause is a clear sign. They’ve already clocked that this isn’t a real app, and every data point collected after that moment is filtered through that awareness.

In financial product testing, the problem is sharper. Finance users are trained to notice when something feels off: a balance that doesn’t add up, a field that accepts anything. When a banking prototype skips real authentication, participants don’t just disengage; they stop mid-session to flag it. The team walks away with findings that reflect how users behave in a demonstration, not in a real product.

The fix is narrower than you’d think. Identify the moment where participant trust is established and make that interaction real. In a banking app, that moment is the login.

This tutorial builds it: credentials that validate, a live error state, and a biometric animation that feels native — no code required.

The login flow, built around Pie Bank, a mobile banking prototype, includes functional text inputs, a masked password field, credential validation, a live error state, and a Face ID animation timed to feel indistinguishable from iOS.

In Figma, open the ProtoPie plugin with your login frame selected and choose Scene when exporting. Flattened collapses everything into a single image; Scene preserves your layer hierarchy so every element arrives in ProtoPie as a separate, targetable layer.

Before moving on: rename every layer meaningfully. “Input Username” not “Rectangle 14”. You’ll reference these names in formulas: vague names compound into real time lost.

ProtoPie’s native Input layer accepts real keyboard entry: participants type actual text, not tap a placeholder. Go to Text  → Input, drag an Input layer onto your canvas, and nest it inside your username field group. Match it visually: placeholder text Username, background fill and font to match your design.

Hit preview. Click the field. Type. That’s the prototype starting to behave like an app rather than depicting one.

Rename this layer Input Username, duplicate it, and nest the copy inside your password field group.

On the duplicated layer, change placeholder text to Password and set Type to Text Password. ProtoPie handles the masking: no custom logic needed.

Preview both fields: username shows text, password shows dots. It already feels real, and you haven’t written a single condition.

Add a new scene, even a blank one. The most common sequencing mistake in ProtoPie is trying to wire a navigation response before a destination exists. Create it first.

Select Log In, add a Tap trigger, set response to Jump, target your dashboard scene, transition Slide in from right to left.

Preview and tap. It navigates: but for any input, including nothing. The prototype is still lying. The next two steps are the fix.

At the bottom-left of ProtoPie, add two Text type variables: username and password. Bind each to its input layer with a formula:

Enable the debug icons: green overlays will show live variable values as you type. When you see your keystrokes appear in real time, the binding is confirmed.

Go back to the Tap trigger on the login button. Add a Condition with two rules, both must be true:

Move the Jump response inside this condition. Wrong credentials, empty fields, wrong format: none get through. Participants now have to actually log in. That single constraint changes the texture of every test session that follows.

Find your error message layer, rename it Error Text, set initial opacity to 0. Add a second condition (the inverse of the first), and inside it, a Change Property response setting Error Text opacity to 100.

Wrong credentials: error appears. Correct credentials: dashboard. Two outcomes: which is what makes this testable, not just demonstrable.

Go to Media, drag a Lottie layer onto canvas, load your Face ID file, and position it off-screen above the iPhone frame. On your Login with Face ID button, add a Tap trigger (rename it Tap Face ID) with four responses in sequence:

Without delays, all four responses fire at once and the scene jumps before the animation plays. Add offsets:

Enable Reset selected scenes on Jump: without it, navigating back leaves the animation stuck at Y: 60.

Preview: tap Face ID, animation drops in, plays, screen transitions. A biometric login indistinguishable from the real thing.

When authentication actually works, the error state becomes a genuine research touchpoint: do users understand the message, do they retry, do they reach for Face ID instead? These are questions a faked login can’t answer.

In stakeholder reviews, the flow speaks for itself. In engineering handoff, the interaction panel documents the behavior (conditional logic, variable bindings, timing) so engineers see intent, not interpretation.

This is why FinTech teams invest in login fidelity even when the login isn’t the feature being tested. It’s where participant trust is established. Get it right, and everything downstream produces better signal.

This tutorial is part of the FinTech Prototyping with ProtoPie series on the ProtoPie blog. The series builds Pie Bank from the ground up across four chapters, covering the dashboard, money transfer logic, and camera integration. If this tutorial was useful, the rest of the series goes further.

“They do not sweat and whine about their condition,” Walt Whitman wrote of the other animals, “they do not lie awake in the dark and weep for their sins, they do not make me sick discussing their duty to God, not one is dissatisfied, not one is demented with the mania of owning things.”

Here was “the poet of the body and the poet of the soul” holding up a mirror to us creatures inhabiting an animal body complicated by a soul — that organ of want and worry which we ourselves invented to explain why we make art, why we fall in love, why we yearn to converse with reality in prayers and postulates.

It is daring enough to ask what a soul actually is. Carl Jung knew that it defies the substance we are made of: “The soul is partly in eternity and partly in time.” Virginia Woolf knew that it defies our best technology of thought: “One can’t write directly about the soul. Looked at, it vanishes.” It is doubly daring to question the age-old dogma that the soul is the province of the human animal alone. Even as we have incrementally and reluctantly admitted other creatures into the temple of consciousness, we have denied them souls — denied them, because our tools of communication and computation have failed to probe it, an inner life capable of imagination and play, of love and grief, of dreams and wonder. And yet our very language defies our denial: the word animal comes from the Latin for soul.

In 1991, long before we came to consider the soul of an octopus, long before fMRI and EEG studies revealed not only that birds dream but what they dream about, Gary Kowalski took up this daring question in The Souls of Animals (public library) — an inquiry into the “spiritual lives” (and into what that means) of whooping cranes, elephants, jackdaws, gorillas, songbirds, horses, dogs, and cats. At its center is the idea that spirituality — which he defines as “the development of a moral sense, the appreciation of beauty, the capacity for creativity, and the awareness of one’s self within a larger universe as well as a sense of mystery and wonder about it all” — is a natural byproduct of “the biological order and in the ecology shared by all life.” (There are in this view echoes of Kepler, who believed that the Earth itself is an ensouled body, and of myriad native cosmogonies that regard other animals as sources of more-than-human wisdom and emissaries of the numinous.)

Kowalski — a parish minister by vocation, who spends his days praying with the dying, blessing bonds of love, and helping people navigate moral quandaries — celebrates the soul as “the magic of life,” as that which “gives life its sublimity and grandeur,” and reflects:

For ancient peoples, the soul was located in the breath or the blood. For me, soul resides at the point where our lives intersect with the timeless, in our love of goodness, our passion for beauty, our quest for meaning and truth. In asking whether animals have souls, we are inquiring whether they share in the qualities that make life more than a mere struggle for survival, endowing existence with dignity and élan.

Many people think of soul as the element of personality that survives bodily death, but for me it refers to something much more down-to-earth. Soul is the marrow of our existence as sentient, sensitive beings. It’s soul that’s revealed in great works of art, and soul that’s lifted up in awe when we stand in silence under a night sky burning with billions of stars. When we speak of a soulful piece of music, we mean one that comes out of infinite depths of feeling. When we speak of the soul of a nation, we mean its capacity for valor and visionary change… Soul is present wherever our lives intersect the dimension of the holy: in moments of intimacy, in flights of fancy, and in rituals that hallow the evanescent events of our lives with enduring significance. Soul is what makes each of our lives a microcosm — not merely a meaningless fragment of the universe, but at some level a reflection of the whole.

Half a century after Henry Beston insisted that “we need another and a wiser and perhaps a more mystical concept of animals,” for they are “gifted with extensions of the senses we have lost or never attained, living by voices we shall never hear,” Kowalski writes:

Without anthropomorphizing our nonhuman relations we can acknowledge that animals share many human characteristics. They have individual likes and dislikes, moods and mannerisms, and possess their own integrity, which suffers when not respected. They play and are curious about their world. They develop friendships and sometimes risk their own lives to help others. They have “animal faith,” a spontaneity and directness that can be most refreshing… all the traits indicative of soul. For soul is not something we can see or measure. We can observe only its outward manifestations: in tears and laughter, in courage and heroism, in generosity and forgiveness. Soul is what’s behind-the-scenes in the tough and tender moments when we are most intensely and grippingly alive.

By investigating the inner lives of other creatures, Kowalski argues, we are invariably deepening our own:

As [modern] shamans, we are allowed to examine enigmas like “What makes us human?” and “What makes life sacred?” We can ask not only about the mating behavior and survival strategies of other animals but whether they have souls and spirits like our own. The danger here is that we are often in over our heads. But at least we are swimming in deep water and out of the shallows. In searching for answers to such queries, I have found, we not only enrich our understanding of other creatures, we also gain insight into ourselves.

There is an inwardness in other living beings that awakens what is innermost in ourselves. I have often marveled, for instance, watching a flock of shore birds. On an invisible cue, they simultaneously rise off the beach and into the air, then turn and bank seawards in tight formation. They are so finely coordinated and attuned in their aeronautics it is as though they share a common thought, or even a group mind, guiding their ascent. At such moments, I feel there are depths of “inner space” in nature that can never be sounded. And it is out of those same depths, in me, that awe arises as I contemplate the synchronicity of their flight. To contain such depths is to participate in the realm of spirit.

We have invented no greater expression of our inwardness than music — the language of the soul, with its eternal translation between mathematics and mystery. We know that other animals partake of that language — each spring birds sing the world back to life, each summer cicadas serenade the sun with their living mandolin, and when we set out to tell the cosmos who we are, a whale song joined Bulgarian folk music and Bach on The Golden Record.

Birds, Kowalski observes, sing for reasons beyond the pragmatic — their song is “far from a mechanical performance” and “much more complex than a simple cry of self-assertion.” It is music, which is distinguished from noise by an organizing principle of creative intent, and creativity may be the purest evidence of soul. Kowalski writes:

Surprisingly, many birds are relatively insensitive to pitch. But the best singers employ all the elements of tone, interval, rhythm, theme, and variation in complex and highly pleasing combinations. And what is music if not the deliberate arrangement of sound in aesthetic patterns?

Greatly influenced by philosopher Martin Buber’s I-Thou model of relating, Kowalski admonishes against relying on our own frames of reference in assaying what other creatures are expressing and how it is being expressed:

The tempo of life is faster-paced for birds than for people. This is one of the reasons the individual notes in bird song are so short, sometimes distinguishable only with a spectrograph, and why the compositions of birds last a few seconds at most, compared to an hour or more for a human symphony. It is also why birds sing in the upper registers (just as the pitch on a phonograph record rises when played at high speed). To the birds, with a metabolism continually in allegro, human beings must appear to be lazy and dim-brained creatures indeed. Just as our music reflects the rhythm and intensity of our inner life, the music of birds expresses the flash and flutter of their nervous and high-strung existence.

Examining another subset of the creative impulse — visual art — Kowalski cites Desmond Morris’s famous 1950s studies, which found that non-human primates given pens and paints not only became adept at using them with “a distinct feel for symmetry and balance,” but developed individual styles of drawing. He considers what that indicates:

Art arises from a spiritual longing that all people share: to make our mark on the world and to spend our life energy in a work that rises above the mundane, adding grace to existence. We respond to the light of the world around us by giving expression to our own inner light, and when the two are on the same wavelength, the world seems more brilliant and finely focused.

Insisting that such spiritual longings do not belong to human beings alone, he cites an astonishing case study:

In 1982 Jerome Witkin, a professor of art at Syracuse University and a respected authority on abstract expressionism, was invited to view a collection of drawings by a “mystery artist.” The professor was busy at the time, preparing for a traveling exhibition. Nevertheless, he was sufficiently intrigued to accept the invitation.

“These drawings are very lyrical, very, very beautiful,” the professor said when he saw the portfolio. “They are so positive and affirmative and tense, the energy is so compact and controlled, it’s just incredible.”

“This piece is so graceful, so delicate,” he said of one drawing. “I can’t get most of my students to fill a page like this.”

Only after he had finished his professional evaluation did Witkin learn the identity of the artist: a fourteen-year-old, 8,400-pound Asian elephant named Siri who lived in Syracuse’s Burnet Park Zoo. Siri’s keeper, David Gucwa, had seen her tracing lines with sticks and stones in the dust of her cage. Against the wishes of the zoo’s superintendent, who scoffed at the notion of an artistic elephant, Gucwa had given her pads of paper and charcoal, permitting her to express herself more freely.

When Witkin showed Siri’s drawings to a colleague without context — an expert on children’s drawings charing the university’s art education department — she firmly concluded that they were not done by a child. Witkin himself readily likened them to the work of Willem de Kooning, wishing the painter himself could see Siri’s art.

It was this report of Siri that inspired May Sarton — one of my favorite poets and favorite thinkers — to reimagine these reckonings in a poem. (The footnote of credit in Sarton’s collection is how I discovered Kowalski’s book.)

The drawings were abstract, Delicate, Like Japanese calligraphy. When the painter de Kooning Was shown them, he said, “Interesting. Not done by a child, I think, Or if so, an extraordinary child.” “The artist is an elephant, Sir, Named Siri.”

It had once come about That the keeper noticed Her sensitive trunk Drawing designs in the dust. After an argument With the head of the zoo Who laughed at him, The keeper himself Brought large sheets of paper And boxes of charcoal And laid them at Siri’s feet. For an hour at a time In happy concentration The elephant created designs. Like Japanese calligraphy. What artist’s hand As skillful As that sensuous, sensitive trunk?

Two decades after Iris Murdoch found psychological symmetry between art and morality, locating in both “an occasion for unselfing,” Kowlaski turns to the acts of selflessness and compassion that evince a moral faculty — that fundament of a soul. Pelicans and crows, he notes, have been known to care for blind comrades. Darwin himself reported of a band of monkeys coming to the aid of member seized by an eagle, at the risk of their own lives. But nothing renders such morally tinted actions more vivid and more moving than one nineteenth-century naturalist’s account of a misfire.

Working in an era when “collecting specimens” meant killing creatures, he aimed at a tern but only wounded the bird, which fell helplessly into the sea. Immediately, other terns began circling above “manifesting much apparent solicitude,” until two of them dove down toward their wounded comrade. They lifted him up, one at each wing, carried him several yards, and gently put him down before another two picked him up, and so the group took turns carrying him the entire distance to the shore. The naturalist was so moved by this display of compassion and solidarity that, although he was within shot of the rock on which the wounded tern had been rested, he couldn’t bring himself to finish what he had set out to do.

To witness such a scene is to be stilled with wonder and with humility — which, as Rachel Carson so poignantly wrote, “are wholesome emotions, and they do not exist side by side with a lust for destruction.” A generation after her, and well ahead of our still dawning awakening to the ecological and ethical dignity of other species, Kowalaski reflects:

If we are to keep our family homestead — third stone from the sun — safe for coming generations, we must awaken to a new respect for the family of life.

We are kin to, and must be kind to, all creation. Overcoming speciesism — the illusion of human superiority — will be the next step in our moral and spiritual evolution.

To behold such a display of moral feeling with our own eyes is stirring enough, but to be witnessed back by another creature’s eyes is nothing short of a spiritual experience. In a passage that calls to mind Alan Lightman’s transcendent account of looking into the eyes of an osprey, Kowalski writes:

It is difficult to probe the inward awareness of another being. The realm of what one mystic called “the interior castle” is wholly private and wrapped in solitude. But when we look into another’s eyes — even into the eyes of an animal — we may find a small window into that inner sanctum, a window through which our souls can hail and greet one another.

The act of making eye contact with another being presupposes a conscious self behind either pair of peepers: I see you seeing me, and I am aware that you are aware that we are looking at each other.

Perhaps in the end it is not we who have the power to acknowledge or deny the souls of other creatures but other creatures who confer soul-ness upon us. Kowalski writes:

If by soul we mean our sense of self, our identity as particular persons, then our souls are interwoven with those of other living beings… We know ourselves as human, in part, through our relationships with the nonhuman world.

We are rather unsure of ourselves. What distinguishes our species may be this inward anxiety. While other animals may be endowed with special gifts—acute hearing, keen eyesight, incredible speed — human beings are nothing special. This is both a biological and a moral judgment. Lack of specialization makes us highly adaptable, but it also means we have no fixed form or definite identity. Without many inborn instincts to guide us, we as human beings need models for how to live. We need a sense of our own possibilities and limits, and we find them not only in the artificial rules and restraints imposed by human society but in the lessons for living suggested by biology and the earth itself. We are the younger siblings in life’s family — the perpetual neonates of the animal world. In a fundamental way we need other creatures to tell us who we are.

Out of this arises an urgency more than ethical, more than ecological, but existential — nothing less than examining what we are and why we are here at all:

What profit do we have if we gain the whole world and lose or forfeit our own souls? The human race may survive without the chimpanzees, orangutans, and other wild creatures who share the planet. But we will have attenuated the conditions that are necessary for our own “ensoulment”… And when we look into the mirror there will be less and less to love.

There is a glimmering of eternity about our lives. In the vastness of time and space, our lives are indeed small and ephemeral, yet not utterly insignificant. Our lives do matter. Because we care for one another and have feelings, because we can dream and imagine, because we are the kinds of creatures who make music and create art, we are not merely disconnected fragments of the universe but at some level reflect the beauty and splendor of the whole. And because all life shares in One Spirit, we can recognize this indwelling beauty in other creatures.

Couple The Souls of Animals with John James Audubon — who was both a visionary ahead of his time and, like the tern-shooting naturalist, a product of its blind spots — on other minds and the secret knowledge of animals, then revisit Loren Eiseley on the wonder of being alive lensed through a bouquet of warblers and a reflection on signs vs. omens and our search for meaning lensed through a great blue heron.

#9432. The Generosity of Selfishness: C.S. Lewis on How to Be Interesting

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

You can also become a spontaneous supporter with a one-time donation in any amount:
