#9398. Comment | People mock Renoir, but painting joy is no easy feat

Purveyor of happiness: Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876) © RMN-Grand Palais/Mathieu Rabeau

“These young people are enjoying life, the beautiful weather, the morning sun shining through the foliage; what do they care about the rest of humanity?” So wrote Georges Rivière, writer and champion of Pierre-Auguste Renoir, of the French painter’s Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876), one of the highlights of Renoir and Love at London’s National Gallery (until 31 January 2027). “They are happy,” Rivière added, “and these are the words that come to mind of all who see this charming painting. None has given me more pleasure than this one.”

“Beautiful”, “happy”, “pleasure”—these terms sit uncomfortably with what John Elderfield, former curator at New York’s Museum of Modern Art, described to the painter Howard Hodgkin as “the modern attraction to difficulty”. Paul Perrin, co-curator of the Renoir show, writes in its catalogue that the “blissful couples and air of happiness” in Renoir’s 1860s to 1880s paintings have made them “immensely popular” yet also prompted “contempt for their apparent lack of complexity and depth”. His assessment was newly confirmed by the critic Eddy Frankel, writing recently in The Guardian: “I’ve hated his work for decades.” For him, Renoir only appeals “when his nudes look like a super-psychedelic, ultra-horny version of Rubens”.

Renoir himself understood that milder emotions irked critics. “It’s hard to get people to admit that a painting can be great painting and still be happy,” he wrote. But love, as framed in this show, has multiple forms, among them empathy. Specialists suggest that Renoir was not ignorant of the “anguished or miserable” elements of life that Perrin describes as being essential to many conceptions of modernity. When Rivière wrote about young people dancing in ignorance of the rest of humanity, he didn’t need to add that happiness can be fleeting and is often most intensely felt at its briefest.

Renoir’s Dance in the Country (1883) © RMN-Grand Palais (Musée d’Orsay)/Hervé Lewandowski

The writings of Baudelaire, and the paintings of Renoir’s peers like Degas and Manet, tell us how visible hardship would have been at the time. And Renoir, unlike those two peers, grew up in working-class Paris, so had lived experience that gave him, as Rivière wrote, “a keen sense of pity” for the poverty of “Montmartre families”. But Renoir clearly felt that if he did want to create great, happy art, he had to avoid troubling subject matter: “There are enough annoying things in life for us not to make more of them,” he said.

Another factor in Renoir’s commitment to joy and play was his deep admiration for what he saw as the golden age of French painting: the Rococo. As Mary Morton writes in the Renoir and Love catalogue, the work of artists like Jean-Antoine Watteau and Jean-Honoré Fragonard “embodied graceful pleasure and a harmonious relationship between the human figure and nature”.

Renoir shares this infatuation with Rococo with a contemporary artist who I think has come closer than anyone else to creating a great art of happiness: Ragnar Kjartansson, whose exhibition Weekdays in Arcadia opens at the Goodwood Art Foundation in Chichester this month (26 November-12 April 2027). Kjartansson told me in 2017 that his fascination with the period lies in the “contrast of really intellectual minds and… silly-billy nothingness”. At Goodwood, he will show No Tomorrow (2022), a video installation that extends his 2017 dance collaboration with choreographer Margrét Bjarnadóttir and composer Bryce Dessner. When I saw the original ballet, in which a group of female performers dressed in jeans and white T-shirts dance with acoustic guitars for the duration of the piece, one moment made me instantly grin: arranged in a grid, every other dancer would take it in turns to leap into the air while the performer next to them stood still, prompting a joyous effect of corporeal effervescence. Kjartansson told me he and Bjarnadóttir felt No Tomorrow was “a Watteau painting in disguise”.

Kjartansson’s most famous piece, The Visitors (2012), a video installation in which he and his friends perform a song in different rooms of a half-derelict mansion in New York State, provokes a similarly ecstatic response from its viewers. But Kjartansson was conscious, perhaps with the reputation of artists like Renoir and of the Rococo period in mind, that he was “in danger of becoming the feel-good artist”. And indeed, part of what makes him such a compelling figure is that the light of his work always comes with copious amounts of shade. At Goodwood, he is interested in “the idea of encountering monuments to sorrow and shakiness in the woodlands”. And yet, I suspect he will find ways to make us smile amid the melancholy.

Achieving joy in art is difficult. Perhaps the most perceptive observer of this fact is one of Renoir’s artistic heirs, Henri Matisse, who spoke of the anguish behind the pleasure in his work: “this happiness, this light and this serene wisdom that [have] seemingly become mine are sometimes earned through the harshness of adversity”. Matisse and, I think, Renoir—like Kjartansson—knew that achieving happiness is a deadly serious business.

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

Where Americans fall on the income spectrum — Pew Research Center 2026 data.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:

The "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

National income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

The FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

The distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, New York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

Pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

#9396. How Psychological Flexibility Can Help Us Belong

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Six ways to move toward connection—even when you feel anxious, awkward, or left out.

The key to belonging may be more within your reach than you think. You don’t need to become more interesting, more confident, or less awkward. You may simply need to become more psychologically flexible.

Psychological flexibility is your capacity to stay present, open to your inner experience, and engaged with what matters to you—even when things feel uncomfortable. Researchers have been studying this capacity for decades, and it turns out that when you are more psychologically flexible, you are not only less likely to struggle with anxiety and depression, you are also more capable of pursuing what matters to you. That might mean repairing  strained relationships, joining the exercise class you feel anxious about, or starting the book club you know would bring more conversation and connection into your life.

Our sense of belonging may be shaped, at least in part, by how we respond to the difficult thoughts and feelings that arise when we reach for connection.

A recent study of more than 16,000 undergraduate students at 104 U.S. colleges and universities found that greater psychological flexibility was associated with a stronger sense of belonging. The study does not prove that flexibility causes belonging, but it points to something hopeful: Our sense of belonging may be shaped, at least in part, by how we respond to the difficult thoughts and feelings that arise when we reach for connection.

Emotional flexibility is your capacity to make room for the range of feelings that can come with being part of a group—whether you’re feeling left out, awkward, or nervous—without becoming overwhelmed by those emotions or needing to suppress them.

Meeting new people can feel awkward, getting past small talk can be tedious, and encountering people with different views can sometimes be irritating.

Sometimes our emotions give us important information. Maybe you are dreading that work event because there’s heavy drinking, and it doesn’t align with your values. That discomfort may be worth listening to. At other times, feeling uncomfortable is simply part of the experience. Meeting new people can feel awkward, getting past small talk can be tedious, and encountering people with different views can sometimes be irritating.

Try this small emotional flexibility practice: Imagine placing the feelings you’re having about a social situation into a backpack. How do you want to carry them? Do you want to shift the weight from side to side? Find someone to help you carry it?  Or perhaps offer yourself some self compassion along the way? You may not get to decide what is inside the backpack, but you can decide how you carry it into your next interaction.

Every so often, look inside. Do these feelings have useful information for you? Do they  need care or attention? If not, adjust the straps and bring them along.

Your mind can be the world’s worst co-pilot when it comes to social situations. It compares you to others, judges you, makes negative predictions and sometimes is just plain mean.

Cognitive defusion is the practice of stepping back from our thoughts rather than automatically treating them as facts.

In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), cognitive defusion is the practice of stepping back from our thoughts rather than automatically treating them as facts.

Before entering a social event, write down some of the thoughts you’re having. Just noting a thought is a thought, helps you get some space from it. You get to decide if you want to take your mind’s advice, or just say thank you and move on.

Try this  cognitive defusion practice: When unhelpful thoughts return, try responding: “Thank you, mind. I know you are trying to help me. And I’ve decided to do this.”

The goal is not to get rid of the thoughts. It is to stop allowing them to make all your social decisions.

When we feel as though we don’t belong, we often see ourselves through a narrow lens: I am not good at conversation. I am the only person who doesn’t know someone here. I never make a good first impression.

You know you are limiting yourself when you use phrases like: I am, I always, I never, I am the only one who…

You know you are limiting yourself when you use phrases like:

I am, I always, I never, I am the only one who…

These kinds of statements can make a passing experience feel like a permanent part of who we are. But pretty much everyone has felt socially awkward at one time or another, and nearly everyone longs to belong. And chances are, you aren’t always this way.

Try this self-flexibility practice: When you notice a  narrow view of yourself taking over, see whether you can become more flexible with your idea of “me.” Can you notice someone else who may be feeling similarly? Can you recognize a way that you are already connected—through your nervousness, or simply by sharing this moment? And can you see yourself as someone who isn’t defined by  “always” and “never”? What changes when you make room for sometimes instead?

In ACT, values describe how you want to show up in your life. They are qualities of action— such as courageously, warmly, playfully, honestly, or presently.

Before entering a social situation, try this values practice. Ask yourself:

If I already felt like I fit in, how would I act?

These questions help you identify how you want to participate and connect with others. You don’t have to wait until you feel confident or included. In fact, the more you act in alignment with your values, the more you may begin to experience yourself as someone who already belongs.

Social anxiety has a way of pulling our attention inward. It shines a spotlight on how we look, whether we’re stumbling over our words, or what might go wrong next.

Try being more flexible with your attention. Notice your feet on the floor, listen to what the other person has to say, or take in the group as a whole. Shifting your focus like this can help you become less caught up in self-consciousness and more aware of what’s happening around you. There’s more to the scene than the words you are saying.

Try this attentional flexibility practice: When you notice yourself getting caught up in comparison or self-judgment, try shifting your attention. What are five things you see? What are four things you hear? What are three things you care about? What are two people you want to meet? What is one thing that matters most to you right now?

When you feel the longing to belong, try acting on it in a small way.

We build belonging one small connection at a time.

When you feel the longing to belong, try acting on it in a small way. At the grocery store, strike up a conversation with the person grabbing lettuce next to you (“What salad are you making?”) At school pickup, get out of your car and wait with other caregivers (“Who’s your kid?”). If you are waiting for a yoga class to start, talk to the person next to you (“Have taken this class before?”) If  someone is sharing the space with you, you already have something in common. It takes courage to make that move, but small gestures like these can open the door to meaningful connections over time.

Use your other psychological flexibility skills to support you! Make room for discomfort, step back from unhelpful thoughts, shift your attention away from self-judgement, broaden your perspective,  and remember why you want to connect in the first place.

Psychological flexibility offers you a greater range of ways to respond, even when you feel like you don’t quite fit in. You can make room for anxiety, step back from your mind’s commentary, widen your sense of self, orient toward your values, return to the present, and make one small move toward connection.

Try out some of these skills, and you will notice, belonging is something you co-create, one flexible move at a time.

Diana Hill, PhD is a clinical psychologist, international trainer and sought-out speaker on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and compassion. Host of the Wise Effort podcast, author of The Self-Compassion Daily Journal, and co-author the ACT Daily Journal. @drdianahill

#9395. Users Don’t Need More Tools: They Need Seamless Integrations

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

We often hear about shiny new tools that change everything (yet again). But in practice, most people don’t need more tools to deal with in their daily lives. What we actually need are better integrations of useful capabilities that neatly align with our existing and established mental models.

Users don’t get excited about shiny new “smart” workflows, or navigating Terminal commands, or jumping between endless back-and-forth chat interactions. They need seamless integrations of useful features to address problems with high severity, high frequency, and a high level of frustration.

I’ve always been puzzled by the notion of “AI-first” products. They might speed up production, but we need to know really well first what we actually want to build. AI-first often doesn’t account for years of small and big design decisions that have shaped expectations and mental models over the years.

I love the notion of “Quiet AI”. These are tools that are mostly invisible, sit in the background, and do small tasks on the user’s behalf. They never scream for attention but happily assist in repetitive, frustrating tasks that can easily be automated or assisted with a smart helper.

Excellent examples of Quiet AI include Claude’s integration within Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, providing assistance in context without disrupting the user’s workflow.

So no wonder that I absolutely love the idea of folder instructions! There, users can define what a folder is supposed to do, based on the purpose they created it for. It sounds much more complicated than it actually is.

The instructions define what the folder is for, how files should be organized, how sub-folders should behave, and what actions can happen inside. Instead of manually maintaining a folder, you set its intent once and let the system follow it.

It’s a seamless integration of AI helpers just when and where users want and need it. With permissions and actions locally scoped to that specific folder on the user’s machine, unless the user extends access, permissions, or system rules on their own.

Note: For a deeper dive into this concept, you can jump to Karthikeya GS’s wonderful post “Folder Instructions: Instructions For System-Level AI”.

User’s value doesn’t emerge from users having to juggle between multiple applications, views, and sources every few minutes. That’s when they are slowed down, and that’s when they make mistakes.

It comes from helping users do the work they need to do — by reducing frustrations, slowdowns and mistakes, and taking care of tasks that otherwise would take too much time and too much effort to complete well.

Yet again, seamless integrations — a very underused but incredibly impactful way to deliver value fast, without adding the burden of installing and learning yet another tool.

#9392. ‘I’m lucky to have grown up around artists’: Cora Sheibani on her path to becoming a jeweller

Cora Sheibani wearing jewellery from her own collections: a bronze bracelet (from Pottering Around collection), Renaissance earrings in platinum and a sapphire facet ring in 18K red gold (both from Facets & Forms Collection)

Art of Luxury magazine, published twice per year by The Art Newspaper, explores how grande marque fashion, jewellery, travel and lifestyle interact with artists, the art market and the museums and heritage sector.

The jeweller Cora Sheibani lives in London and works from a small studio in Mayfair. She was raised in the art world—her father was the celebrated Swiss dealer Bruno Bischofberger, who collaborated with artists including Jean-Michel Basquiat, Andy Warhol and Francesco Clemente. As a dyslexic, Cora did not embrace reading as a child, but now she explains why it is her window on the world.

For me, luxury is about having time. As you get older, and as the world gets faster, there’s never enough of it. In an ideal world I would travel more, both for work and for pleasure; and visit exhibitions, galleries and museums. But I also have a son who needs a lot of my attention—he is very autistic, with severe ADHD—and so I travel through books, and reading has become a way to experience culture, art and creativity.

I’m lucky to have grown up around artists and people who didn’t follow the conventional path. Francesco Clemente is a close family friend, and his daughters are more like my cousins. We’re close to the Schnabel family; Jean Tinguely was my sister’s godfather. So even though I barely read as a child—it was just too hard—I made myself study liberal arts before I became a jeweller. Only after university I started reading German literature. It’s my mother language, after all.

I’ve always loved jewellery. When I was 15, I worked in my parents’ gallery over the summer, and spent half my earnings on two rings, both bronze, one Greek, one Roman. Now I work primarily with gold: at first it was because yellow is my favourite colour, but you also learn that gold is the friendliest metal to handle.

It was hard to be taken seriously as a jeweller at the beginning. People thought it was a hobby, and I really had to be patient and persevere—that’s something I can do, that dyslexia taught me. Now I’m incredibly proud of my work and how successful the business has become.

Jewellery books and especially exhibition catalogues are a real inspiration. An essay by Amin Jaffer in the catalogue for Joyaux Dynastiques, a show at the Hôtel de la Marine in Paris last year of royal jewels, explained the meaning of a particular kind of nine-gem Indian jewel. It really helped me with a commission I’d just received from a client for a piece using nine different coloured stones.

I buy some early editions from Shapero Rare Books in Mayfair—I pass it every time I go from the gym to the studio and can’t resist taking a look. I just finished reading Crime and Punishment by Fyodor Dostoyevsky in its first English translation by Frederick Whishaw. It’s very rare, a real collector’s item. It’s generally thought that translations have improved, but there’s something special about reading a contemporaneous one. It’s a rich experience that takes you back in time.

Once a month, I get together with my book club. There’s only three of us, and we don’t all have to read the same book. Instead, we talk about what we are each reading. We meet, usually on a Friday morning, at Daria Buchman’s house, and have a breakfast of scrambled eggs. Daria, with her husband Dimitry, sponsors the International Booker Prize, so she is really on top of every new novel. She hadn’t read Beloved by Toni Morrison, though. I’d read three works that talked about slavery from different regional angles—Beloved, Crooked Plow by Itamar Vieira Junior and Ben Okri’s The Last Gift of the Master Artists—and recommended to my group they did the same. You begin to understand a bit better how the lives of people from one continent evolved in such different (and at times similar) ways. On the other hand, Daria made me read the wonderful Wuthering Heights. I wouldn’t have done it if she hadn’t insisted.

#9391. What Poetry Can Teach Us About Wonder: An Interview With Maya C. Popa

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

An interview with poet Maya C. Popa on attention, uncertainty, and the art of remaining curious.

We often associate wonder with extraordinary experiences, moments of beauty or awe that stop us in our tracks. But what if wonder is also a way of paying attention, one that invites us to question what we think we know and remain open to what we cannot immediately understand?

Poetry offers a particular way of exploring this possibility. It asks us to slow down, look more closely, and make room for ambiguity, uncertainty, and experiences that resist easy explanation. In doing so, poetry may have something to teach us about presence, curiosity, and our capacity to find meaning in the world around us.

What if wonder is a way of paying attention that invites us to question what we think we know and remain open to what we cannot immediately understand?

Poet Maya C. Popa has spent years exploring wonder through her doctoral research and her creative work. Her collection Wound Is the Origin of Wonder examines wonder beyond beauty and astonishment, while her newest collection, If You Love That Lady, explores the ways attention and experience can challenge our assumptions. In this conversation, Popa reflects on the relationship between poetry and mindfulness, the value of questioning our perceptions, and how cultivating wonder might deepen our connection to the world around us.

As a fellow graduate of NYU’s Creative Writing Program, I’ve had the opportunity to work with Maya over the past several years and follow the evolution of her writing. The author of three poetry collections and three chapbooks, and founder of the Conscious Writers Collective, she has devoted much of her creative and scholarly life to exploring how wonder shapes our  experience of the world.

Angela Stubbs: You’ve spent years exploring wonder both as a scholar and as a poet. Having lived with the subject for so long, how has your understanding of it changed??

Maya C. Popa: I’ve become more sensitive to how “wonder” is used conversationally, often as a substitute for admiration, surprise, or delight. It’s understandable, of course, because wonder can share qualities with the sublime or awe-inspiring. But my PhD focused specifically on the idea that wonder leads us to ask questions, which is where I think its true power lies.

My intention was to study wonder not merely through an aesthetic or critical lens, but as a fundamental human aptitude.

If we look at wonder’s etymology, it’s clear it’s not a tidy, straightforward, or uncomplicated experience. It derives from the Old English wundor, which some scholars have suggested may be related to German wunde or wound. The noun form means a surpassing or breach of the mind’s faculties, while the verb form means to demonstrate a state of admiration or astonishment, or to search for understanding or meaning. “The verb wonder,” writes scholar Daniel Fusch, “indicates an emotional response to a marvelous incident; the noun wonder indicates both the name for that response and the marvelous incident that provoked it…That is, at the sight of a wonder, we wonder; such are the beautiful complications of the English language.”

My intention was to study wonder not merely through an aesthetic or critical lens, but as a fundamental human aptitude that we could cultivate that ultimately serves as a vehicle for curiosity and empathy. Of course, I also believe it’s vitally important to live in a state of appreciation and gratitude, but wonder’s stakes and demands are psychically fascinating and deserve to be considered closely by teasing out these semantic distinctions. This allows us to fully own the power of wonder, not just treat it as another modern buzzword.

Angela Stubbs: You’ve spoken before about wonder as involving both knowing and not knowing. In the opening poem of If You Love That Lady, “At the Entrance of a Love Poem, I Hesitate,” there’s a sense that arriving at an answer can actually end the inquiry. What interests you about keeping a question alive? Is there something poetry allows us to experience by resisting the impulse to resolve or explain too quickly?

Maya C. Popa: Poems unearth and discover as they go; they are, as our wonderful Nobel Laureate Anne Carson suggests, “an action of the mind captured on a page…a movement of yourself through a thought, through an activity of thinking.” Wonder catalyzes the poetic impulse. I do think it provokes a generative restlessness that naturally seeks its shape in language.

I also believe that wonder can be passed from writer to reader.

I also believe that wonder can be passed from writer to reader. As Peter de Bolla suggests in his study of aesthetic experience, literary works of art are produced through the activity of reading. It makes sense—as we read, we’re responding in our heads as we metabolize it. Reading is inherently interactive, especially for writers.

So, to answer the question more directly, I absolutely believe in the value of keeping the question alive, and I think part of our sense of aliveness comes from that feeling of ongoing inquiry into life. Rilke advised the young poet to “Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves.” We can witness the results of our need for immediate resolution, certainty, and shortcuts everywhere in our culture. It’s at the heart of some of our greatest concerns (artificial intelligence, GLP-1s, etc.). There are an increasing number of ways around critical thinking. Sitting with, even taking as much enjoyment in the question as the solution, feels like an essential part of thinking and writing to me.

In the case of the opening poem, I wanted to begin with a self-interrogation that acknowledged the recurrence of love poems throughout history, and the ways that the beloved always seems to be situated at a distance, inviting the poet to write towards them to close the gap. Then there’s the notion, also helpfully introduced by Anne Carson, that desire requires a gap. So, this collection reflects a great deal on these questions.

I always think of Lucille Clifton saying that poems come out of wonder, not out of knowing.

Angela Stubbs: Throughout this collection, perceptions are revised: a mouse becomes a wren, a hawk moth is mistaken for a hummingbird. Do you see wonder as a willingness to discover that our first perceptions, or the stories we tell ourselves, are incomplete? Does this relate, in some way, to the writing process, which requires a similar receptivity? How do you know when to direct a poem and when to follow what it is becoming?

Maya C. Popa: I always think of Lucille Clifton saying that poems come out of wonder, not out of knowing. I value that kind of mental flexibility and capacity to revise one’s thinking or perception instead of stagnating or atrophying around a belief. That openness and capacity to evaluate and reevaluate as needed is invaluable to poets, who do this regularly throughout the process of revising. I certainly wanted to pay attention to this capacity when I noticed it in myself and deliver it on the page as precisely as I could. As a poet, I often feel I’m acting both as the lightning and the bottle that captures it at the same time.

Practically, I have to listen very closely for the deeper and more interesting questions beneath the surface of my writing as I go. What drove me to the page may not be what interests me by the end of many drafts. All of this requires me to set my ego to the side and be ruthlessly honest when something is not working, either because it isn’t rigorous or precise enough in its thinking, or it hasn’t yet found its music.

It’s rare that I’ll have a poem come together over only a handful of drafts; it’s more likely that I’m working on several poems over the course of a year or two, and many I will never share.

This requires me not to know for a lot of the time, and then, as I discover and distill what I’m doing, to make that discovery legible first to myself, and then hopefully to the reader. This takes revision in layers over many months or years. That is about the time it takes for me to really understand my own sound-sense on the page. It’s rare that I’ll have a poem come together over only a handful of drafts; it’s more likely that I’m working on several poems over the course of a year or two, and many I will never share.

Angela Stubbs: In “February Clear,” you turn from looking at the natural world toward the possibility that looking itself can change us. What is the difference, for you, between merely seeing something and giving it the kind of attention that might actually alter the person who is looking?

Maya C. Popa: I always think of the adage that we see things not as they are, but as we are. I also think that we often show up with our psyches in 12 different places at once. How often are we thinking of the thing we have to do next, the irritating conversations that we just had, what other people are doing on the internet, etc? It’s hard to stay in our own lane, and in our own moment.

[A]ttention and importance are also relayed and understood through language. If ours is significantly limited, how can we advocate for the natural world?

In that poem, I was trying to capture the experience of looking and really seeing, and acknowledging how often that isn’t the case. As someone who did not grow up with an agrarian vernacular, I also acknowledge that while my ancestors might have looked at green spaces and immediately conjured a palette of words for what they noticed, I can only name a handful of any landscape’s features. And those are mostly the obvious things: the hills, the grass, the rocks. I can’t name the kind of tree or type of grass. And this matters, because attention and importance are also relayed and understood through language. If ours is significantly limited, how can we advocate for the natural world? My friend, the extraordinary naturalist Robert Macfarlane, says that “we will not save what we do not love, and we rarely love what we cannot name.”

Angela Stubbs: We often talk about “cultivating wonder,” particularly in mindfulness and contemplative spaces, as though wonder were something we could deliberately produce. After studying and writing about it for so many years, do you think wonder itself can be cultivated, or can we only cultivate the attention, openness, and receptivity that allow us to recognize it when it appears?

If we treat wonder as being purely positive, as being in constant admiration, we will so often fall prey to our moods, which will make it hard or make it feel forced.

Maya C. Popa: I think we absolutely can and should cultivate a sense of wonder. But if we come back to its purpose as being partially to drive us to ask questions, not just to admire, I think we’re closer to the thing that actually counts, which is not taking things for granted. If we treat wonder as being purely positive, as being in constant admiration, we will so often fall prey to our moods, which will make it hard or make it feel forced.

Cultivating wonder initially involves paying attention a bit more deliberately than we usually would, before it becomes a kind of natural orientation. It’s slightly different from a gratitude practice, although it also gets us out of our sense of routine and shows us what is quite unlikely, the “marvelous singularity” of our human experience.

Rachel Carson said that “the more clearly we can focus our attention on the wonders and realities of the universe about us, the less taste we shall have for the destruction of our race,” and I stand by her thinking that wonder and humility are what safeguard us from egregious destruction. If we can wonder at the unlikeliness and distinctiveness of a human life, then we’re less likely to turn to violence. The more we develop our capacity to wonder, the greater our art, certainly, and the greater the hope that we will see our interconnectedness and protect and value each other.

Angela Stubbs is the founder of Pitch Perfect Media, a PR company dedicated to amplifying the voices of women and visionaries shaping culture and change. She holds dual MFAs in Creative Writing—one in Fiction from the Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics at Naropa University, and one in Poetry from the Creative Writing Program at NYU Paris—where her studies in contemplative education and poetics deepened her meditation practice. Angela leads heart-centered meditation offerings in Los Angeles and is currently at work on a poetry manuscript exploring memory, surrender, and the art of letting go.

#9390. Designing For Distressed Users: Why Mental Health Apps Shouldn’t Follow Every UI Fashion

Kat Homan is a product (UX/UI) designer at DŌBRA Studio. She designs B2C mobile and web products, including four mental-health products and have prior … More about Kat ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Mental health applications keep facing a continuing, measurable crisis: many people stop using them quickly. The data is stark: almost 95% of users who open the app on day 1 abandon the app by day 30, with a median 30-day retention of only 3.3%. Even the recognised mental health giants lose around 50% of their users within the first ten days. This severe engagement loss and retention collapse are why effective interface design must be a clinical and operational priority. Good design is not merely aesthetic; it is a fundamental tool for user retention.

While many factors drive this abandonment, research suggests that mental health apps have tended to prioritise visual appeal at the expense of what actually sustains users. In a space defined by vulnerability and cognitive strain, chasing visual fashion risks adding effort when users have the least to spare — quietly trading away the utility and trust the app depends on. Users don’t open mental health apps out of curiosity, but from need — often while stressed, anxious, overwhelmed, or exhausted. In these states, an unconventional icon, a confusing gesture, or a flashy animation instead of a delightful surprise becomes an extra cognitive overload. Moreover, it becomes a reason to disengage.

In those moments, visual experimentation from a mild distraction can turn into a friction that undermines the very help the app is meant to deliver. A solution must be a visual interface that is simple in usage and understanding from the first moment.

Crucially, improving engagement depends less on which UI trends you follow than on a single test applied to each one of them: does a trend lower the cost of using the app when the user can least afford it?

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

Before we look into the specific problems, we must recognise a core tension: many UI trends are optimised for goals that mental health apps don’t share.

Pursuing the former directly overrides the latter. It’s not a surface-level error of colour or font; it’s a foundational conflict of purpose. This tension surfaces across five fronts, each a place where adopting a trend on novelty alone can cost more engagement than it seeks to create.

The proposed principles are not based on a single A/B test or one isolated study. They are built from published research on mental health app engagement, cognitive load, accessibility, and emotional response in mHealth, set against competitive product audits and app-store evidence, and pressure-tested against my own quantitative and qualitative product work. That last source I treat as an illustration, understanding the limits of personal experience. In this context, validation is less about proving that one interface pattern universally works and more about asking whether a design reduces effort, preserves agency, avoids emotional mismatch, and remains usable when the user is already under strain.

A note on the examples: This isn’t a ranking of apps. Every app has its own positioning, target audience, constraints, and business pressures that may not be visible from outside, and a pattern that strains a user in distress may be exactly right for that product’s actual goal. I’m reading individual, visible design decisions for one question only: how they might affect someone arriving in a low-capacity state.

The primary goal of any mental health tool is to reduce, not increase, cognitive load. Yet, many trendy interfaces achieve the opposite. Neo-brutalist layouts with stark contrasts demand visual parsing. Hidden navigation menus that rely on non-standard swipes turn simple tasks into puzzles. Abstract, unlabeled icons force users to guess rather than recognise. Each of these patterns adds friction — seconds of hesitation, a moment of confusion — and for a user whose mental energy is already low, those costs start to accumulate.

This friction is most damaging during acute need. Research suggests that when a user is in a state of high anxiety or depression, even typing or making simple choices can feel overwhelming. When an interface demands high cognitive effort at the moment support is needed, it doesn’t just make that session harder — it gives an overwhelmed user a reason to close the app, and a reason not to reopen it. Each point of confusion can become a place where a user may quit for good.

Other findings show that apps with simple interfaces reduce the time and effort required to engage, directly improving retention. Conversely, a complex, trend-driven UI increases that time, creating an obstacle course that undermines the very healthy habit formation the app is meant to support.

This does not mean that every mental health product must be visually plain or minimal. The issue is whether the interface meets the user’s current capacity.

A panic-support tool, for example, works best when it offers a small number of obvious actions, rather than asking the user to browse. However, if a calming action meant for a moment of panic instead surfaces an upgrade screen, the product fails the user at precisely the point where failing matters most. Monetization is not the issue by itself; the issue is whether it appears at a point where the user expects immediate support.

Nonori shows the same principle in a more reflective context. The app does not present the user with a large content library or a complex dashboard at the start. Instead, it leads them through a simple, linear sequence of small actions. The value of this pattern is that it reduces the effort needed to begin. When a user is tired, anxious, or mentally overloaded, knowing exactly what to do next can lower the barrier to returning.

At the other end of the spectrum, comprehensive tracking apps show a different trade-off. Bearable, for example, is genuinely powerful: it consolidates almost everything a person tracks — mood, symptoms, sleep, medication, habits, reports, correlations — into one place. For users managing chronic conditions or preparing for medical appointments, this can be genuinely useful. But the same comprehensiveness can become a burden for an exhausted user. Dense dashboards and multi-step check-ins require executive capacity — the very resource that anxiety, depression, burnout, or brain fog often reduce.

A similar tension appears in anxiety apps with strong support content but busy entry points. A product may contain useful features yet still make the first screen feel noisy with too many cards, locked items, playful characters, or upgrade prompts. This is not evidence that the product is bad. It shows how the same interface can feel very different depending on the user’s state: clear enough during exploration, but too demanding during distress.

This insight shaped a guiding principle for our work: every interaction point must meet users at their current level of capacity, removing mechanical and cognitive barriers rather than adding to them. This principle guided our integration of low-friction, state-aware interactions in apps like Bear Room, a stress and anxiety reduction app, and Teeni, an emotional-wellbeing app for parents of teens.

In Bear Room, we already had a fast mood-based flow built around four emotion cards. At the same time, our product research supported a second need: users also wanted more personalised support. We avoided making this a long selection flow or a typing-only route because both can still create friction for people under stress or anxiety. Instead, we made voice a primary, prominent path, always alongside a text alternative. A central microphone button allows users to share what’s on their mind. The app then uses AI to analyse the input and provide a tailored set of coping practices.

Rather than picking a single entry model, we kept two paths because they served different states. That matched what we saw in later analytics and user conversations: quick emotional selection worked better when users wanted speed, while open voice or text input worked better when they wanted personalisation and to feel more heard. This was more a pattern we noticed, without having the exact measured results.

Similarly, in Teeni, we directly addressed the cognitive friction of parenting stress by introducing a “Quick Relief” button. This creates an empathy-friendly flow for parents experiencing anger or frustration. The button initiates a dedicated “Hot Flow,” allowing them to first vent and relieve their immediate negative emotions through voice input. Only after this emotional release does the app gently guide them into the more reflective “Cold Flow” for the rest of the app’s resources. This sequential, state-sensitive design acknowledges that a user in peak distress cannot navigate a complex app; they need a direct, simple, and validating first step.

These solutions directly tackle cognitive friction by meeting users at their level of capacity, resisting trends that add visual or interaction complexity. Voice input and single-action buttons remove the mechanical and cognitive burden of navigation and typing. The result is an interface that feels reliably non-judgmental and genuinely helpful when users are least equipped to navigate complexity.

A user’s emotional state is the context in which a mental health app operates. This is why its visual language must be empathetic and considerate. Research investigating how colour and aesthetics influence mood in mHealth apps suggests a critical insight: users in distress show a strong preference for subtlety. They long for dark palettes, sleek and sophisticated looks, and clean, uncluttered aesthetics, explicitly noting that cheerful, bright colours, while seemingly appropriate, can create a jarring, even physically uncomfortable conflict with their current mood.

This does not mean that every mental health or wellbeing app should look dark, quiet, or clinically restrained. The category is broad: it includes self-care, anxiety support, habit change, addiction recovery, trauma tools, therapy-adjacent products, and apps for more severe mental health contexts. A playful visual style may be appropriate for one product and a poor fit for another. What matters is not whether the interface is bright or muted, but whether its emotional tone fits the product’s purpose and the likely state in which users arrive.

Emotional mismatch can also appear in mechanics, not only in aesthetics. In Calmer, an anxiety and panic relief app, the interface itself appeared relatively clean and relaxed. Yet some of its engagement and monetisation mechanics sit in a different register from that relaxed: a discount wheel, or confetti celebrating a logged low mood. For a user who just recorded a hard moment, that shift — from quiet support to upsell or celebration — can land as a mismatch, whatever its intent.

For Bear Room, we prototyped a “cosy room” design informed by direct feedback from our users, which echoed the study’s conclusions. Several users in our research described the apps they had tried for similar needs as “too bright, too happy, and too overwhelming”. Users longed for a digital safe space. This was part of what pointed us toward a quieter palette in the final design: muted, earthy tones — neutral hues like soft greens and taupes — set against darker, calming backgrounds. For this product — a refuge for users arriving overwhelmed — that meant a middle ground: a space that feels safe without being gloomy. The interface avoided any bright alerts or sudden animations, making calmness the core feature.

This case underscores a critical principle: an overly cheerful, bold, or trend-forward interface can feel dismissive to someone in distress, creating a conflict that erodes trust. As Bear Room shows, trust is built when the interface respectfully aligns with the user’s emotional reality, offering solace through subtlety (which creates an overall feeling of a “welcoming and safe atmosphere”), not a solution through saturation.

Mental health often relies on routine and predictability. Yet many contemporary UI trends thrive on novelty and disruption, intentionally reimagining fundamental navigation. When an app introduces a novel interaction pattern, such as a unique swipe or a non-standard button behavior, it asks the user to learn something before they can act, forcing them into cognitive effort they can’t afford.

This does not mean that mental health apps must be plain, rigid, or generic. A product can have its own character, playfulness, and sense of identity. The question is whether that identity remains understandable and predictable when the user returns in a low-capacity state. A gamified self-care app like Finch may work well when the user arrives ready to explore, play, and build a routine. But open it after a hard day just to mark one task done, and the can’t-skip celebration screens that delight an engaged user become one more layer to get through before they reach what they came for.

A similar tension appears in large meditation and wellbeing platforms. Apps such as Headspace and Calm offer extensive libraries of different content. This breadth can be valuable during exploration. But in moments of stress, the product question becomes sharper: can the user return and immediately find the exact support they need, or do they have to search, filter, and relearn the structure?

Someone experiencing anxiety or executive dysfunction needs to use the tool in a straightforward navigation manner, not an interface they have to learn each time anew.

PTSD Coach, a public-health-oriented trauma-support app designed to help users learn about and manage symptoms after trauma, offers a useful positive example. Its interface is not trying to be fashion-forward. Its strength lies in a stable information architecture: users can learn, track symptoms, manage symptoms, and get support through clearly separated areas. For a user returning during distress, this predictability matters more than novelty.

CALMzone offers another useful example. Some of its breathing animations differ from standard visual patterns, but they remain tied to the exercise itself: the animation shows what to do, when to inhale, and when to hold. The guided audio screen also explicitly invites the user to put the phone down and listen. This is a rare and valuable form of interaction design: the product’s success is not more screen time, but reduced effort and regulation.

These insights guided our approach in applications like Bear Room, where navigation reliability was treated as a therapeutic feature. We intentionally crafted an experience of an empathetic guided flow.

Recognising that users would likely approach in states of overwhelm, we structured the interface as a clear, unwavering path, with a visible “Start” sign. Key emotional support tools here are represented as the room’s objects — symbols of daily life, unmistakably recognised by all. They are visually highlighted by design so that the user won’t get lost in the elements, can easily access the needed tool, and can remember their way around the digital space upon the next return to the app.

Trend-driven interfaces sacrifice this navigational certainty for novelty. Each unconventional choice in mHealth apps, when core functions are buried behind experimental interactions or placed in unexpected locations, leads to a cumulative effect of fatigue instead of innovation. Users are not in a place to explore. They abandon the entire practice of seeking digital support when every interaction feels like solving a new puzzle. This does not restrict experimentation; it simply means that animations, micro-interactions, AI, or playful mechanics must serve the user’s state rather than interrupt it.

Many popular UI trends can be exclusionary when applied without adaptation. The minimalist trend of low-contrast text fails users with visual impairments. Gesture-only navigation marginalises those with motor difficulties. Visually dense, animated interfaces can overwhelm users with cognitive or attentional conditions. In mental health, the population needing support disproportionately includes individuals with these accessibility needs.

Choosing a trending aesthetic over an accessible one is therefore an active decision to limit the app’s reach and efficacy. It ensures that those who might benefit most cannot use the tool effectively. Accessibility isn’t a layer you add at the end; it’s a constraint you design within, with most of it codified in Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2. Body text needs 4.5:1 contrast against its background, large text and interface elements 3:1 — exactly what low-contrast minimalism fails. Interactive targets need a floor of 24×24 px (more for unsteady hands). Every gesture needs a visible button fallback, or you risk excluding anyone who can’t perform the swipe.

A final, and often overlooked, consequence of trend-following is the adoption of engagement mechanics designed for entertainment, educational, or productivity apps. Features like streaks, aggressive notifications, and gamified reward systems are engineered to maximise screen time and create dependency. Although they have long been considered effective tools for increasing retention, in a mental health context, this approach can easily be misguided. What presents as “motivation” can quickly transform into a source of performance pressure and guilt. For a user managing depression, a broken streak or a missed daily goal can exacerbate the very feelings the app aims to alleviate.

These mechanics are not inherently unethical. In routine-building products, they can help some users. The risk appears when they are transferred into mental health contexts without adapting for shame, low energy, relapse, and non-linear recovery. A streak, for example, is not just a retention mechanic when the user is emotionally vulnerable. It can become a visible record of whether they have “kept up” with their well-being.

In the apps I reviewed, this tension appeared through familiar persuasion patterns: streaks, streak freezes, commitment copy, urgency-based notifications, “don’t miss this offer” prompts, and success-framed buttons such as “Yes, I want to succeed.” In self-care or wellbeing products, these details can make the app feel less like a supportive tool and more like another system the user has to satisfy.

Designers still need return triggers. A mental health app has little value if users install it once and forget it exists. But return mechanics must be adapted to the emotional context. In Bear Room, for example, this philosophy is embodied in short, forgiving three-day streaks: the streak does not reset when a user misses a day, and every third day brings a small benefit. The goal is not to punish absence, but to gently support return.

The same principle applies to lighter interactions. Bear Room includes a simple, optional bubble-popping game. Its purpose, however, is not to hook the user but to offer a brief, calming interlude. It is deliberately finite, providing a small mood lift and gently signposting other resources within the app. The value is in the momentary relief, not the extended session.

This commitment to supportive, non-coercive design extends to foundational app architecture:

In mental health technology, sustainable retention is earned not by capturing attention, but by becoming a consistently respectful and helpful presence in a user’s life.

The mHealth apps design invites finding a challenging balance between boosting their use without being too demanding.

This is not a niche concern affecting a fringe audience. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that about one billion people globally live with a mental disorder, with depression alone affecting nearly 5% of adults. Critically, the overall number is rising — in the last decade, depression and anxiety cases have increased by 25%. This vast and vulnerable population cannot afford for its tools to fail due to poor design. While UI trends aren’t inherently problematic, their application within wellbeing products demands a radically contextual approach.

Even a five-minute decompression tool between meetings has an emotional context, and a style chosen for its look — glassmorphism, a certain flavour of ultra-minimalism — can miss it, however sophisticated the audience. The point isn’t that these styles are wrong; it’s that the look has to answer to the moment. Soft biomorphic shapes or fluid transitions can genuinely help when they directly serve the goal of calm — and the same elements become noise when they’re there to impress.

The five fronts outlined above are not just a diagnostic lens; they are the foundation of an evaluation framework for anyone designing in the mental health space. Before incorporating any trendy visual or interaction pattern, it is worth running it through each of them in sequence:

A design that passes all five holds together as something more than usable: it becomes a tool that users can trust enough to return to in moments of genuine need.

Trends can be inspiring. They can win awards and generate buzz. But in mental health, sometimes the best design is the one that helps users feel understood — a quiet helper they trust enough to return to in moments of stress and vulnerability. It doesn’t steal the spotlight, but focuses on the user’s emotions. In the end, the ultimate goal is not for the interface to be seen — but for the support to be felt.

#9389. How to Cope With Loneliness: 5 Mindfulness Practices to Feel More Connected

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Feeling lonely isn't a personal failing, and you don't have to transform your social life overnight in order to feel more connected. Try these five gentle mindfulness practices.

I live in a rural area, about four miles from my nearest neighbor. My husband works away on a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rotation, which is fairly common where I live. The community is widely scattered, you need a car to get almost anywhere, and there isn’t a great deal of interaction between neighbors. In fact, I suspect many people don’t even know who lives closest to them.

But I want to make something clear: I’m not generally a lonely person.

Loneliness doesn’t only find people with empty calendars or empty houses. It looks different for everyone.

At school, I was labeled a “loner.” I’ve never had a large circle of friends, preferring instead the company of two or three close ones. Those friendships have lasted through the years and many birthdays. Two of my closest friends live in the UK, and we keep in touch through online chats, time difference and all.

#9388. Elisha Goldstein: A Nourishing Breath Meditation

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

The deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are. This simple awareness of breath practice is an act of self-love and compassion for the moment we find ourselves in.

Mindful breathing often serves as the foundation for meditation practices because your breath is always with you, wherever you are, and it can be used as an anchor to the present moment. In essence, all that’s involved is simply being mindful when you breathe in and out. There is no need to analyze, count, visu­alize, or manipulate the breath in any way. Just breathe normally and naturally and be aware of breathing in and out. There are a few methods you can use to focus on your breath. You can be mindful of your breath in your nose, chest, belly, or even your entire body as it breathes in and out.

With any of these practices, the deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are.

For dealing with the challenges of stress and anxiety, we sometimes recommend abdominal breath­ing—breathing from the belly, rather than only into the chest—as this can be very calming. However, if another location is preferable, please listen to your own wisdom. Generally speaking, abdominal or belly breathing is the way we all naturally breathe, especially when we’re lying down. To determine if you’re breathing from your abdomen, place your hand on your belly and feel whether it expands as you inhale and contracts as you exhale. If it doesn’t, turn your attention to breathing more deeply and feeling your belly expand and contract with your breath.

An important benefit of abdominal or belly breathing is that it helps moderate irregular breathing patterns, which often arise due to stress or irritation. Anxiety can lead to shallow, rapid, or sporadic breathing and even hyperventilation, and a full-blown panic attack can cause increased shortness of breath, thoughts of losing control, and pains in the chest. By bringing the breath back into the belly, you can help the body return to balance. So when anxiety arises, first acknowledge the feeling, then gently bring attention to the abdomen and practice mindful belly breathing.

Before we begin, we have one final bit of advice: With any of these practices, the deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are. This might mean simply noticing and acknowledging stress or anxiety rather than falling into old patterns of running away from it. You may discover that by embracing your fear you find your heart.

Do this practice in a relaxing environment without distractions, such as the phone. You can do it either lying down or sitting up, but if you lie down and find yourself falling asleep, try a more upright posture. Bring your full, undivided attention to this practice as you listen or read the following meditation, pausing after each paragraph. You can practice anytime throughout the day, combining this practice with the mindful check-in if you like.

Read and practice the guided meditation script below, pausing after each paragraph. Or listen to the audio practice.

This practice excerpted from A Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Workbook, by Bob Stahl and Elisha Goldstein. New Harbinger Publications

Elisha Goldstein, Ph.D., is a clinical psychologist and conducts a private practice in West Los Angeles. He is founder of the Mindful Living Collective—a donation-based leading global network for mindful living and learning, and creator of the Uncover the Power Within coaching program and the free master class on the Uncover the Power Within Blueprint. He is also the author of Uncovering Happiness: Overcoming Depression with Mindfulness and Self-Compassion (Atria Books, 2015), The Now Effect (Atria Books, 2012), Mindfulness Meditations for the Anxious Traveler (Atria Books, 2013), and co-author of A Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Workbook (New Harbinger, 2010).

#9387. Aros museum in Denmark acquires sun-like Olafur Eliasson sculpture in new partnership with the artist

Olafur Eliasson's Presence (2025), installed at the Queensland Art Gallery and Gallery of Modern Art in Brisbane

Photo: Chloë Callistemon © QAGOMA Courtesy of the artist; neugerriemschneider, Berlin; and Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, New York © 2025 Olafur Eliasson

The Aros Aarhus Art Museum in eastern Denmark will acquire a major piece by the high-profile Danish-Icelandic artist Olafur Eliasson—a crowd-pleasing vast glowing yellow sphere that appears to hover in space (Presence, 2025)—as part of a new long-term partnership.

The initiative between the artist and the museum, called “Shared Futures”, also encompasses Thin Ice, a solo exhibition to open autumn 2027. “This exhibition presents key works from recent decades alongside new projects reflecting Eliasson’s growing engagement with the climate, ecology, and humanity’s relationship with its surroundings,” says a statement.

A new site-specific version of Eliasson’s installation Waterfall (2004) will meanwhile be installed on Aros’s Art Square from 9 October next year; Studio Olafur Eliasson will also create a publicly accessible library collection of books on Eliasson’s artistic production at Aros under the plans. In addition, the partnership includes a dedicated postdoctoral research position in collaboration with Aarhus University.

Eliasson's Waterfall (2019), installed at Tate Modern in London

Photo: Anders Sune Berg; Courtesy of the artist; neugerriemschneider, Berlin; Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, New York © 2019 Olafur Eliasson

Eliasson says in a statement: “Aros has supported my work in Denmark for many years, so it felt natural to make my online archive and library available there… the ambition is to show that museums can offer depth and focus for engaging with an artist’s practice in a more detailed, granular way.” The museum is also home to Eliasson’s rainbow rooftop walkway Your Rainbow Panorama (2011).

Eliasson's Your rainbow panorama (2011) at Aros

Tina Sørensen © Schmidt Hammer Lassen, 2026

Rebecca Matthews, the museum's director, tells The Art Newspaper: “I first met Olafur Eliasson when I was chief executive of the European Capital of Culture in 2017, when he created an extraordinary stage design for the performance Tree of Codes. We were supposed to have our photograph taken together, but it was pouring with rain, so we ended up standing in a colonnade, talking. I remember thinking: If I ever get to lead a museum, he will be the first person I call.” Matthews became director of Aros in 2022.

In December 2025, Eliasson appeared on The Art Newspaper podcast A brush with…. with Ben Luke. “His works can be deceptively simple or enormously complex, but often share a rigorous and reductive geometry, which may conversely produce expansive and multifarious perceptual, sensory and embodied effects,” wrote Luke.

Site-specific installation called Life opened this week at the Fondation Beyeler near Basel in Switzerland and can be visited at all hours

Artist's Tate Modern retrospective features works drawn largely from European collections in an effort to reduce carbon footprint
